title: Liability of the Administration — Tortious and Contractual

content.overview: The State and public authorities may incur tortious and contractual liability. Sovereign immunity has been substantially narrowed; the State is generally liable for torts committed by its servants in the course of employment, subject to recognised exceptions and statutory immunities.
content.glance: Identify the act (sovereign vs non-sovereign); test employment and course of employment; check statutory immunity; state the remedy (damages, specific performance limits).
content.study: Classical sovereign immunity no longer bars ordinary tort claims against the State for negligence of its servants. Courts distinguish sovereign functions (historically immune) from non-sovereign commercial or service functions (liable). Contractual liability of the State is governed by ordinary contract principles subject to constitutional and statutory constraints on government contracting. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the Constitution, the relevant statute and established Supreme Court authority. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of liability doctrine.

sections.heading: Tortious Liability
sections.body: State liability for torts of servants in the course of employment; sovereign/non-sovereign distinction narrowed but still relevant in some contexts.

sections.heading: Contractual Liability
sections.body: Government contracts bind the State subject to constitutional and statutory limits; specific performance and damages follow ordinary principles with public-law overlays.

sections.heading: Immunities and Limits
sections.body: Statutory immunities, limitation, and the distinction between public-law remedies and private-law damages.

sections.heading: Remedies
sections.body: Damages, declaration, and in appropriate cases public-law relief under Articles 226/32.

provisions.title: Suits and proceedings by or against the State

examples.title: Negligent driving by government servant
examples.body: A government driver negligently injures a pedestrian in the course of official duty. Tortious liability of the State is ordinarily engaged.

examples.title: Breach of government contract
examples.body: A public authority repudiates a concluded commercial contract without justification. Contractual liability and, where arbitrariness is shown, public-law review may both be available.

hypotheticals.question: Is the State immune from all tort claims?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Sovereign immunity has been substantially narrowed; ordinary negligence in the course of employment generally attracts liability.

hypotheticals.question: Can contractual liability be combined with Article 14 review?
hypotheticals.analysis: Yes, where the State’s contractual conduct is also arbitrary or discriminatory, public-law remedies may supplement private-law claims.

distinctions.title: Tortious vs contractual liability of the State

misconceptions.trap: The State is never liable in tort.
misconceptions.correction: Sovereign immunity has been substantially narrowed; ordinary employment-related torts generally attract liability.
They are enforceable subject to constitutional and statutory constraints.

cases.name: State of Rajasthan v Vidyawati
cases.facts: Tort claim against the State for negligence of a servant.
cases.issue: Whether the State is liable for torts of its servants.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The State can be liable for torts committed by its servants in the course of employment; classical immunity is not absolute.
cases.relevance: Foundational authority on State tort liability.

cases.name: Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.facts: Claim arising from acts characterised as sovereign functions.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Distinction between sovereign and non-sovereign functions was applied; later authority has narrowed the immunity.
cases.holding: Immunity applied on the classification adopted.
cases.relevance: Historical authority on sovereign functions; subsequent case law has limited its reach.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a State-liability problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the act and the servant. II. Test course of employment. III. Check sovereign/non-sovereign classification and statutory immunity. IV. State the remedy.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Facts of the wrong; employment link; immunity analysis; damages or public-law relief sought.
